name: Emeka Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a small brass band, record short saxophone parts for local adverts and teach five teenagers. My master’s in music helps me read a difficult chart, but keeping a band together is mostly showing up early and paying players when promised.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What goes into making that possible at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works rotating bakery shifts, and we arrange pickup for our two school-age children around the band calendar. The leader’s fee is low for the responsibility, our mortgage is fixed, and savings cover only about two weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the band that a quicker booking form is useful if it leaves us more time to rehearse. I would still insist on a written fee for every player.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two weeks of savings makes a late venue payment dangerous now. There are few similar band-leader jobs nearby, so a quiet AI future does not settle my household bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I would lead the booked brass sets, record paid horn lines and teach the five teenagers. I use AI daily for rehearsal lists, but I check each name, time and musical instruction myself before sending one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel anxious about payment delays even in this mild picture. I would not feel safe until the venue fees land in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened at the last late-paying venue?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hall paid us nine days after the agreed date, and I covered the players first. Before the next date I would request a deposit large enough to pay every player, in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask family to cover the gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could ask my brother for a lift, but I will not ask him to fund the band. A player’s wage has to come from the booking.

I would request a **player-covering deposit** before the next hall date.
think: Our **two-week reserve** makes late venue payment dangerous.
Few **local band posts** would replace this low-paid lead work quickly.
do: Keep **booked brass sets**, paid horn lines and five pupils this week.
Request a **written deposit** covering every player before the next hall date.
feel: I feel **anxious** about existing late payments and the mortgage.
S0.quote: A player’s wage has to come from the booking.
fieldNote: He pays **band members first** and has only two weeks of household savings.
Existing **daily AI lists** receive his manual checks before musicians see them.

steps.text: Keep booked brass sets, paid saxophone recordings and five pupils
Request written hall deposit covering all players before next date

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the advertisers that generated horn lines may be cheap, but a live brass band still needs a leader. I would ask the hall for contracted paid dates rather than hold Saturdays on trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Advert parts make up almost a third of my pay, and those calls could be the first to go. Band nights and lessons are real, but I cannot replace a lost recording week with goodwill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I would request three months of written paid hall dates and a paid session with the studio engineer on its new note-separation tool, which isolates notes from a recording. In the first year I would test that tool on a saxophone take I own only after the engineer approves local storage; I would compare every note by ear and stop if the rhythm changes or the file leaves the studio.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about losing adverts. Two weeks of savings are not enough to prove a new product works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you test it on a pupil’s solo?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. No teenager’s name or recording goes into the tool; my own nameless take gives me enough to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if hall dates shrink as well?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep teaching and seek a posted paid house-band leader job only if the lost dates are real, my degree qualifies, its written net fee after travel beats the lost pay and pickup fits; I would not leave until an offer is signed. I would ask the venue to send me the posting before applying.

Apply for a **posted band role** after lost dates only if qualified, written net after travel beats loss and pickup fits.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a realistic loss of recording fees.

Keep paid brass dates and pupils until suitable written offer is signed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the band that AGI by 2028 can make a recorded horn line before I open the case. I would ask venues to sign dates and deposits while people still book us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect advert recordings to disappear in 2028 and some halls to choose generated backing instead of a full band. Robots that can carry and play instruments arrive about three years later, around 2031. Our paid band dates can fall before a playing robot appears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would total advert invoices and ask for a signed hall calendar with player deposits. In the first year after 2028, if paid band nights fall too, I would apply for a posted arts-centre brass tutor role only if my master’s qualifies, written net pay after travel replaces the lost band fees and pickup fits the bakery rota; I would keep paid band and pupils until an offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel anxious about losing advert fees with just two weeks saved. If adverts and halls both fell, I would be alarmed because together they are most of my pay. I have lain awake thinking about the players and mortgage, but I can still seek a real paid post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you borrow to buy a better recording setup?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only with a signed paid recording order covering the gear and player costs. I would not put a speculative kit on the mortgage card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the arts-centre role is just a conversation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep working until a real vacancy is posted with written hours. A conversation is not a wage.

Keep **paid band and pupils** until a suitable written offer is signed.
feel: I feel **anxious** about expected recording loss; losing live work too would alarm me.
S2.quote: Our paid band dates can fall before a playing robot appears.
fieldNote: His **2028 advert losses** precede capable playing robots around 2031.
The **tutor move** depends on actual hall cuts, qualified posted vacancy, written net pay, pickup and signed offer.

steps.text: Apply for qualified posted tutor after 2028 cuts; written net after travel replaces fees, pickup fits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the young players that five years until AGI by 2031 is time to learn to repair the instruments we already have. A working horn is worth more than another generated advert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Advert income may end by 2031, and playing robots could come around 2034. A paid repair trade could steady work, but I will not buy a course merely because the name sounds safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This autumn I would seek a funded brass-repair apprenticeship only if a workshop offers a real place, paid hours and a schedule that fits pickup without cutting my partner’s bakery shifts. In the first year after 2031, if advert fees fall, I would apply for a posted paid instrument-repair job only if the apprenticeship qualifies me, its written net pay after travel covers lost fees and pickup works; I would keep band and pupils until a written offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious until a repair wage is real. I can work with my hands. Two weeks of savings cannot buy a new trade by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you repair a child’s horn on day one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would work under the shop mentor, check each repair before it goes out and leave safety-critical soldering to a qualified repairer until I am signed off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the place is funded but unpaid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I would keep the booked brass work and ask about the next paid intake. Free tuition cannot replace my share of the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the band that ten years before AGI by 2036 is time to make paid work dependable. Apprentices should be paid to learn, and leaders should not call late wages experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Advert fees could disappear by 2036 and robots may handle live instruments around 2039. I can seek a better-paid brass lead post, but our two-week reserve is an immediate problem even if both dates slide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this month I would save five percent of each extra paid pupil fee after the mortgage, food and band wages, aiming for two months of expenses, and require written deposits that cover the players before each venue date. In the first year after 2036 I would apply for a posted arts-centre brass lead job only if my music master’s qualifies, its written net pay after travel covers lost advert and band fees and pickup fits; I would keep paid band and pupils until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stay anxious because one late hall cheque can exhaust our savings now. A decade gives me time to qualify, but it does not pay the players this Friday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there are no extra pupils?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I add nothing to savings that week. I cannot save fees nobody has paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take an unpaid brass leadership title?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I need a written wage, work hours and real pickup coverage before I leave the band.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because advert and hall fees might fall together. Signed paid dates, a real qualified tutor opening and pickup compatible with bakery shifts would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whose money pays the band first when a venue is late. I cannot call myself a leader and leave the trumpet player unpaid.

headlineQuote: I cannot call myself a leader and leave the trumpet player unpaid.
portrait: At **43**, Emeka leads brass players, records saxophone adverts and teaches five teenagers with a music master’s.
His **lower pay**, two-week reserve, mortgage and few local band posts make late venue fees urgent.
He uses **AI daily**, yet tests a new studio tool only after paid training, approved storage and listening checks.
A **paid repair apprenticeship** offers another route only with funded tuition, wages and pickup without lost bakery pay.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove advert fees and reduce paid halls before another role appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed hall dates**, a qualified posted tutor opening and pickup fitting bakery shifts would help Emeka.
